2335968.title: Department of Telecommunications Organises First All India Conference on Official Language 2026 in New Delhi
2335968.body_html:
Ministry of Communications
Department of Telecommunications Organises First All India Conference on Official Language 2026 in New Delhi
Posted On: 13 NOV 2026 6:24PM by PIB Delhi

The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) organised its First All India Conference on Official Language 2026 today at Dr. Ambedkar International Centre, Janpath, New Delhi, with the objective of promoting the progressive use of Hindi as the Official Language in official functioning and governance.

The conference commenced under the guidance of Shri Manish Sinha, Member (Finance), Department of Telecommunications as the chief guest. The inaugural session featured the lighting of the ceremonial lamp by the chief guest along with other dignitaries present on the dais. Member (Finance), Advisor(T), Advisor(O), Deputy Director General(C&A), Joint Secretary (Admin), CGCA addressed the gathering and highlighted the importance of promoting the use of Hindi in official work. The inaugural session was followed by the welcome of the distinguished speakers.

The first session featured deliberations by Shri Kumar Pal Sharma, Dr. Om Nishchal and Shri Rajesh Srivastav, who shared their perspectives on various aspects of the use, promotion and enrichment of Official Language Hindi. The second session focused on the policies, provisions and tools related to Rajbhasha Hindi, with insights from Smt. Kiran Bharadwaj and Shri Saurabh Arya.

The conference witnessed active participation from dignitaries, officers and officials of the Department of Telecommunications and its attached, subordinate and autonomous offices, along with non-government members. The discussions provided a platform for exchanging ideas and experiences on strengthening the implementation and progressive use of Hindi in official communication and administrative work.

The conference concluded with a vote of thanks by Shri Kamal Swaroop, Deputy Director (Official Language). Shri Hemant Kumar, Assistant Director (Official Language), and other officials of the Department of Telecommunications played an active role in organising and ensuring the successful conduct of the conference.

The Department of Official Language, Ministry of Home Affairs, regularly organises All India and Regional Official Language Conferences to encourage the progressive use of Hindi in accordance with the constitutional provisions and the spirit of Article 351 of the Constitution of India. The Parliamentary Committee on Official Language also emphasises such initiatives to strengthen the use of Hindi in governance and public administration. In this context, the Department of Telecommunications has taken this initiative forward by organising its first All India Conference on Official Language, reaffirming its commitment to promoting Rajbhasha Hindi in official functioning.

2335961.title: Vice-President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan addresses valedictory session of 31st CII Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam
2335961.body_html:
Vice President's Secretariat
Vice-President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan addresses valedictory session of 31st CII Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam
Vice-President calls for translating investment commitments into tangible outcomes; lauds Andhra Pradesh’s development trajectory
Andhra Pradesh emerging as a major gateway for India’s global economic engagement: Vice-President
India aspires not merely to participate in the emerging global economic order but to play a leading role in shaping it: Vice-President
Posted On: 13 NOV 2026 6:13PM by PIB Delhi

The Vice-President of India, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan, today addressed the valedictory session of the 31st edition of the CII Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh.

The Vice-President appreciated the remarkable development achieved by Andhra Pradesh under the leadership of Chief Minister Shri N. Chandrababu Naidu.He noted that the State had attracted 714 investment projects worth over ₹22 lakh crore since June 2024, reflecting strong investor confidence and economic momentum.

He said that the State’s vision of Swarna Andhra 2047 was aligned with Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Investments in green energy, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum technology, ports, aerospace and advanced manufacturing were positioning Andhra Pradesh as an emerging industrial and innovation hub.

Referring to the theme of this year’s Summit, ‘Navigating the New World Order – Trade, Technology and Trust’, the Vice-President observed that geopolitical uncertainties, technological disruptions, climate change and evolving supply chains were reshaping the global economy. However, every period of uncertainty also presented new opportunities, and nations demonstrating adaptability, innovation and trusted partnerships would be best placed to shape the future.

He expressed confidence that India, under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, was moving firmly towards becoming a developed nation by 2047. Emphasising India’s growing economic strength, young and skilled workforce, vibrant entrepreneurial ecosystem and expanding manufacturing and services sectors, he said that India aspired not merely to participate in the emerging global economic order but to play a leading role in shaping it.

The Vice-President highlighted the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum computing, biotechnology, advanced manufacturing and digital platforms. He stressed that Atmanirbhar Bharat should not be understood as turning inward, but as building domestic capabilities, enhancing competitiveness and integrating more deeply with global markets.

Calling for a collective national endeavour towards Viksit Bharat 2047, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan emphasised that the responsibility of building a developed India could not rest with the Government alone. It required the active participation of industry, academia, entrepreneurs, young people and international partners, in keeping with the Prime Minister’s call for Sabka Prayas.

Concluding his address, the Vice-President called upon stakeholders to move from dialogue to action, from opportunity to achievement, and from partnership to shared prosperity. He expressed appreciation to all participating countries, international delegates, industry leaders and institutions for their contribution to the Summit.

The Governor of Andhra Pradesh, Shri S. Abdul Nazeer; Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, Shri N Chandrababu Naidu;Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy, Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, and Education, Shri Pralhad Joshi; Union Minister for Civil Aviation, Shri Kinjarapu Ram Mohan Naidu; Andhra Pradesh Ministers Shri Nara Lokesh and Shri T. G. Bharath; CII Director General Shri Chandrajit Banerjee; and CII President Designate Dr. Suchitra Ella, among other dignitaries, were present on the occasion.

2335948.title: English rendering of PM’s address at the inauguration of COSMOS-Mysuru Planetarium in Mysuru, Karnataka
2335948.body_html:
Prime Minister's Office
English rendering of PM’s address at the inauguration of COSMOS-Mysuru Planetarium in Mysuru, Karnataka
Posted On: 13 NOV 2026 5:57PM by PIB Delhi

My Greetings to everyone!

Governor of Karnataka, Sudha Yadav Ji, Chief Minister D. K. Shivakumar Ji, my Cabinet colleague, Nirmala Sitharaman Ji, Minister in the State Government, Basavaraj Rayareddy Ji, my colleague in Parliament, Yaduveer Krishnadatta Chamaraja Wadiyar Ji, all the scientists, researchers, teachers, other distinguished dignitaries, and my dear brothers and sisters of Mysuru.

First of all, I respectfully bow to Tai Chamundeshwari. I am very happy to be here in Mysuru once again. Just a few months ago, I had come among you for the inauguration of the Viveka Smaraka. And today, we have gathered here to dedicate the COSMOS Planetarium to the nation. Both these occasions convey a profound message about India's values and our culture. Viveka Smaraka inspires us to look within ourselves and seek spiritual knowledge. At COSMOS, on the other hand, our eyes are lifted towards the sky. We are inspired to explore this vast universe and understand its mysteries. This is an example of how the traditions of spirituality and science in India have always progressed side by side.

Friends,

Our ancestors used to study the sky very closely. They understood the movements of stars and planets, prepared calendars and calculated the timings of solar and lunar eclipses. India was home to many great astronomers such as Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Bhaskaracharya and Nilakantha Somayaji. The advanced instruments and technologies that are available today did not exist at that time. Despite this, they made great discoveries and carried out even the most difficult calculations.

Friends,

Mysuru has a tradition of establishing institutions that encourage the pursuit of knowledge. The University of Mysore was established during the reign of Maharaja Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar. The Wadiyar family also played an important role in laying the foundation of the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. These institutions have provided generations of students and researchers with opportunities to advance. And today, when India is achieving one milestone after another in the field of science, Mysuru, too, is adding a new chapter to India's scientific journey in the form of this state-of-the-art COSMOS Planetarium. Today, this state-of-the-art COSMOS Planetarium is being dedicated to the youth and the people of the country. It is India's first LED Dome Planetarium. I have just had the opportunity to watch a show here. It was a remarkable experience in itself. I congratulate the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, the University of Mysore, various government departments and everyone associated with its construction. I extend my congratulations to the nation on this occasion.

Friends,

For a long time, there has been a call in our country, which Nirmala Ji mentioned in her speech just now - Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan. Atal Ji added Jai Vigyan to it, and then I added Jai Anusandhan as well. The India of the 21st century is moving forward with this very vision. And our country's youth are performing exceptionally well in this regard. Last year, India hosted the International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics in Mumbai. Our young people participated in it with great enthusiasm. And this year, for the next edition of the same Olympiad, five students from India went to Vietnam. Four of them won gold medals and one won a silver medal. This is a matter of pride for the entire country.

Friends,

Our young students are also performing remarkably well in other fields of science. This year, Indian students achieved major successes in the International Olympiads as well. These included subjects such as Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry and Biology. All the students won either gold or silver medals. This has been a record achievement for India. This means that when our youth get opportunities, when they receive the necessary resources to learn, and when they get the support of technology, tools and institutions, they demonstrate their ability to achieve great things. This COSMOS Planetarium, too, is now going to help them greatly in giving shape to their dreams.

Friends,

Technology is changing the world very rapidly today. And no country can afford the risk of moving slowly in this area. Over the past decade, India has made unprecedented progress in astronomy, astrophysics and the space sector. We have installed new telescopes in the country. In several challenging areas of space exploration, India has today become one of the few countries in the world. Through Chandrayaan-3, ISRO made India the first country in the world to land near the Moon's South Pole. In the form of Aditya-L1, India has received its first solar observatory in space. Just last year, India became the fourth country in the world to demonstrate the capability of docking and undocking in space.

Friends,

During this period, an Indian also reached the International Space Station and conducted several new experiments. The experience gained from this mission is also proving useful for our own human spaceflight programme, Gaganyaan.

Friends,

Our government opened up the space sector. This created new opportunities for the private sector. India's startups also got an opportunity to demonstrate their capabilities. Today, our youth are launching their own rockets, placing satellites into orbit and undertaking many such activities in the space sector that had never been carried out in India before. This is the scientific approach of a New India, where new discoveries are being encouraged, new technologies are being developed and new opportunities are being created for our youth.

Friends,

India has always moved forward with the mantra of Humanity First. India's space missions, too, have been dedicated to the welfare of humanity. For example, ISRO has developed a satellite communication system for our fishermen brothers.

With the help of this system, when boats equipped with receivers are at sea, officials can send timely alerts to them during storms. And they can also track their safe return to the shore.

Friends,

Many of you must be checking the live location of trains. This tells you where a train has reached and when it is expected to arrive at a station. This information is provided by the Real-Time Train Tracking System developed by Indian Railways and ISRO. Similarly, satellite data is also used in the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana. Under this, information collected from fields, along with satellite data, is used to estimate crop yields. Farmers' insurance claims are being determined on the basis of these estimates. This means that today, our satellites are reaching the heights of space, while at the same time, they are being used to improve people's lives on Earth.

Friends,

Science for Society- this is our approach. We are continuously promoting research and innovation in the country. More than one crore students have so far benefited from the country's over 10,000 Atal Tinkering Labs. These labs provide children with opportunities to work on their ideas, conduct new experiments and innovate.

Friends,

To advance research, it is essential that our students and researchers have access to the world's best research. With this objective, we launched One Nation One Subscription. It is now greatly helping the country's educational and research institutions gain access to leading scientific journals from around the world. We established the Anusandhan National Research Foundation. Through this, we are helping an increasing number of universities undertake new research.

Friends,

Last year, we also launched a Research, Development and Innovation Scheme worth Rs. 1 lakh crore, so that our country's researchers continue to receive adequate funding. This is helping take new technologies out of laboratories and bring them to practical use.

Friends,

Today, a strong ecosystem for science and research is taking shape in the country. Curiosity among young people is essential for making progress in the field of science. Planetariums and science centres play an important role in nurturing this curiosity. I urge everyone associated with COSMOS to work in this area so that schools and colleges here can organise visits for as many students as possible, and arrangements can be made to bring them here. The children who come here to learn about the universe may well be among those who return here one day and tell us about the new discoveries they have made about the universe. And that will be the greatest achievement of this COSMOS Planetarium. With this confidence, I wish you all the very best for the journey ahead. I extend my best wishes to all of you. Thank you very much.

DISCLAIMER: This is the approximate translation of Prime Minister’s address. Original address was delivered in Hindi.

*******

MJPS/SS/VJ/ST

2335913.title: Union Health Minister Shri J.P. Nadda reviews institutional progress of Rural Health Training Centre (RHTC), Najafgarh
2335913.ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
2335913.body_html:
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Union Health Minister Shri J.P. Nadda reviews institutional progress of Rural Health Training Centre (RHTC), Najafgarh
Shri J.P. Nadda Commends RHTC Najafgarh for Its Commendable Progress and Strengthening of Institutional Infrastructure and Healthcare Services
RHTC records over 94,900 OPD visits and nearly 36,000 emergency cases between August and October 2026
Centre strengthens primary healthcare network through three Urban Primary Health Centres and their Sub-Centres
Posted On: 13 NOV 2026 5:32PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare Shri Jagat Prakash Nadda today reviewed the institutional progress and development of the Rural Health Training Centre (RHTC), Najafgarh, New Delhi, under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

During the review, the Minister was apprised of the progress made by the institution across hospital and patient care services, diagnostic and support facilities, human resources, academic infrastructure, quality assurance and community-based healthcare delivery.

Addressing the gathering, Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare Shri J.P. Nadda appreciated the commendable work undertaken by RHTC Najafgarh in strengthening its institutional infrastructure and healthcare services. He observed that the institution was progressing in the right direction and commended the efforts of the RHTC team in taking forward its development initiatives. He also acknowledged the significant contribution of Safdarjung Hospital and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in supporting the institution's growth and development. He expressed confidence that the continued efforts and collective commitment of all stakeholders would further strengthen RHTC as an important centre for patient care, medical education and community healthcare.

Strengthening Hospital and Patient Care Services

RHTC Najafgarh has recorded substantial patient footfall during the August–October 2026 period. The institution attended to 94,927 patients in its Outpatient Department (OPD) across 10 specialities and provided emergency services to 35,985 patients. The hospital recorded 198 inpatient admissions during this period.

The institution also performed 691 surgeries, comprising 101 major and 590 minor surgeries. Its Anti-Rabies Centre and the Snake Bite Treatment facility also provided substantial service during the same time span.

The hospital has functional labour rooms, a pharmacy with an updated formulary of over 350 medicines, and dedicated Ayurvedic and Dental Clinics, further broadening the range of services available to patients.

Expansion of Diagnostic and Support Infrastructure

The review also highlighted the strengthening of diagnostic and support services at the institution. The laboratory is NABL-accredited, while the Ultrasound (USG) facility became operational on October 24, 2026, and has conducted 148 scans. The Physiotherapy and Audiometry units are functional, with 252 audiometry tests conducted between August and October 2026.

Other important facilities, including the Central Sterile Supply Department (CSSD), Effluent Treatment Plant, Sewage Treatment Plant and Medical Gas Pipeline System, have also been completed.

The institution is working towards operationalising the Blood Storage Unit and Mortuary by January 2027. The CT Scan and X-ray facilities are planned to become operational during the first quarter of 2027.

Focus on Academic Infrastructure and Quality Assurance

RHTC has also strengthened its nursing education and training infrastructure. The ANM Training School has been renovated, with an annual intake capacity of 44 students for its two-year course. The institution also has an ANM hostel with a capacity of 60 beds.

The institution has undertaken quality improvement initiatives under the National Quality Assurance Standards (NQAS) for its three Urban Primary Health Centres. Of the 129 identified action points, 105 have been completed, while 24 are in progress. State-level evaluation and certification are targeted for December 2026, followed by national-level evaluation from February 2027 onwards.

The institution has also completed several important compliance-related activities, including biomedical waste management certification from the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), e-waste management and Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) compliance. Energy, fire, structural and safety audits have been completed, while the water audit is in progress.

Future Development Roadmap

The review also covered the institution's short-, medium- and long-term development plans. In the short term, RHTC aims to operationalise specialised clinics, including Thalassemia, De-addiction, Adolescent Health, Venereal Disease, Rheumatology and Non-Communicable Disease clinics by December 2026.

The medium-term roadmap envisages the establishment of teaching departments in Family Medicine and Emergency Medicine, with a target of operationalisation by the end of the first quarter of 2027. The longer-term vision includes the development of a B.Sc. Nursing College, Allied Health Sciences College, residential hostel and expansion of medical education facilities.

The process of upgrading RHTC into a 230-bedded hospital is already underway. The proposed expansion is expected to strengthen its capacity for patient care, medical education and institutional training.

The review also covered key operational requirements, including the availability of specialists, senior residents and other healthcare personnel, along with infrastructure and administrative matters necessary for the institution's further development.

About RHTC

Established in 1937, RHTC Najafgarh has a longstanding legacy of service, education and community healthcare. The institution provides comprehensive primary healthcare services through three Urban Primary Health Centres (UPHCs) at Najafgarh, Ujwa and Palam, along with their respective Sub-Centres. These facilities cater to the healthcare needs of the rural and peri-urban population, with a focus on maternal and child health, immunisation, family welfare and disease control programmes. The centres also serve as practical training facilities for medical, nursing and paramedical students.

The progress at RHTC Najafgarh reflects the continued efforts towards strengthening accessible, comprehensive and quality healthcare services, while developing institutions that integrate patient care, medical education, skill development and community health.

*****

2335903.title: Ministry of Culture Convenes "Creative India: Collective Possibilities" at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi; Invites Partners to Build India's Creative Economy Together
2335903.body_html:
Ministry of Culture
Ministry of Culture Convenes "Creative India: Collective Possibilities" at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi; Invites Partners to Build India's Creative Economy Together
Posted On: 13 NOV 2026 5:28PM by PIB Delhi

The Ministry of Culture, Government of India, today organised "Creative India: Collective Possibilities", a conference on collaborative models for India's creative economy, at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. Inaugurated by Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, Hon'ble Union Minister for Culture, the Conclave brought together representatives of the Central and State Governments, the Ministry's institutions, industry, philanthropy, the creative community and international partners, to explore how India's cultural wealth can contribute more fully to growth, livelihoods and India's place in the world.

"The creative power of India is its real power," said Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat. "Ours is a living civilisation, whose creativity belongs to every region and every generation. As the world turns to an economy of ideas and imagination, our task is to connect this talent with opportunity, so that India's culture becomes a foundation of its prosperity and of its voice in the world."

"Government's role is to be a catalyst," said Shri Vivek Aggarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Culture. "When the Ministry opens the door and partners carry the work forward, our heritage becomes a living resource for communities, artists and enterprise alike. The Creative Economy Division has been created to build exactly these partnerships."

Setting the context, Shri Inderjeet Singh, IAS, Joint Secretary (Creative Economy), placed culture at the heart of India's development agenda, from the Kashi Culture Pathway to the vision of Viksit Bharat. He described the Ministry's 43 organisations, from more than 3,600 protected monuments to museums, archives, Akademis and Zonal Cultural Centres, as the public infrastructure of India's creative economy. As custodian of India's heritage, collections and living traditions, he said, the Ministry offers a natural meeting point for the many sectors, enterprises and creators that draw on India's culture.

Partnerships are already in motion. The National Culture Fund has completed 66 projects with 39 partners since 1996, and Adopt a Heritage engages partners at 66 monuments. The sacred Piprahwa relics returned home through a partnership with Godrej Industries Group, Sabhyata Foundation has brought cultural evenings to Purana Qila, and the India Pavilion at Venice 2026 was realised with the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre and Serendipity Arts Foundation. A new MoU with Google Arts & Culture will carry India's heritage to audiences worldwide.

Four sessions, on Investing in Culture, Culture-Led Spaces, Culturepreneurs, and Technology and Communication, brought patrons, investors, heritage practitioners, designers, entrepreneurs and technology leaders into conversation. The deliberations explored trusted routes for philanthropy and private capital, monuments, museums and festivals as living destinations, pathways from livelihood to enterprise for artisans and designers, and new ways of carrying India's knowledge and narratives to the world on India's own terms.

The takeaways from the day will inform the Ministry's continued engagement with States, institutions and partners, in India and abroad.

The Ministry envisages a common and evolving framework for India's creative economy, grounded in measurable outcomes, simpler facilitation and structured routes for capital into culture. Guided by the principle of convening, facilitating and enabling, the Ministry invited its partners, from State Governments and cultural institutions to industry, philanthropy, creators and the international community, to shape this framework with it and to work with its institutions in turning India's heritage and living traditions into lasting livelihoods, enterprise and global presence.

***

2335867.title: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs Special Campaign 6: 736 Public Grievances Redressed, 448 MP References Disposed of and 25,070 Files Reviewed
2335867.body_html:
Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs
Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs Special Campaign 6: 736 Public Grievances Redressed, 448 MP References Disposed of and 25,070 Files Reviewed
526 cleanliness campaigns conducted; 10,551 square feet of office space freed
Scrap disposal generates ₹2.50 lakh; 100 percent PMO references disposed of
Posted On: 13 NOV 2026 4:53PM by PIB Delhi

Special Campaign 6, undertaken during October 2026 by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs  recorded significant achievements in reducing administrative pendency, strengthening record management and promoting cleanliness in government offices. The campaign focused on the disposal of pending references, redressal of public grievances, review of physical and electronic files, simplification of rules and processes, and management of e-waste.

Disposal of Pending References and Redressal of Public Grievances

As on 31 October 2026, 736 public grievances were redressed, 448 references from Members of Parliament were disposed of, and 100 Percent PMO references were disposed of. In addition, seven Parliamentary Assurances were addressed and one State Government reference was disposed of.

These activities formed part of the campaign’s efforts to reduce pendency and promote responsive administration.

Review of 25,070 Files to Strengthen Record Management

A total of 25,070 files were reviewed, comprising 16,217 physical files and 8,853 e-files. The exercise supported systematic management of official records and identification of files for retention or disposal in accordance with applicable procedures.

526 Cleanliness Campaigns Conducted; 10,551 Square Feet of Space Freed

During the campaign, 526 cleanliness campaigns were conducted to promote cleaner and better-organised workplaces.

Disposal of scrap and obsolete materials, along with weeding out of old files, freed 10,551 square feet of office space, making it available for more effective utilisation.

Scrap Disposal Generates ₹2.50 Lakh

The campaign generated ₹2,49,656 in revenue through disposal of scrap, including e-waste. Of this amount, ₹40,036 was generated through e-waste disposal.

E-waste management activities covered 77 units, supporting efforts towards responsible disposal of obsolete electronic materials.

Four Rules and Processes Identified for Simplification

As part of the drive to improve administrative efficiency, four rules and processes were identified for simplification.

Special Campaign 6 reinforced the importance of integrating cleanliness, timely disposal of pending matters and systematic record management into routine office functioning. The campaign’s achievements reflect continued efforts towards efficient use of public resources and responsive, citizen-centric governance.

2335853.title: NLMC Announces E-Auction of Residential Flat in Kilpauk, Chennai; Pre-Bid Meeting Rescheduled to 28 November 2026
2335853.body_html:
Ministry of Finance
NLMC Announces E-Auction of Residential Flat in Kilpauk, Chennai; Pre-Bid Meeting Rescheduled to 28 November 2026
RFP released on 5 November 2026 for residential property at Poonamallee High Road, Kilpauk, Chennai, with a reserve price of ₹1.64 crore
Corrigendum issued on 13 November 2026 revising the Pre-Bid Meeting to 28 November 2026 at 11:00 AM
Posted On: 13 NOV 2026 4:37PM by PIB Delhi

The National Land Monetization Corporation (NLMC), a wholly owned Government of India company under the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), Ministry of Finance, has announced the e-auction of a residential flat located at Poonamallee High Road, Kilpauk, Chennai, Tamil Nadu.

The Request for Proposal (RFP), bearing No. NLMC/2026/01, was released on 5 November 2026 as part of NLMC's initiative for the e-auction of 12 residential flats located in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh, and Chennai, Tamil Nadu.

The residential property at Kilpauk, Chennai, has a reserve price of ₹1.64 crore and offers prospective buyers an opportunity to acquire a residential asset in an established locality of the city through a transparent and competitive e-auction process.

Pre-Bid Meeting Rescheduled to 28 November 2026

NLMC has issued Corrigendum 1 dated 13 November 2026, revising the date of the Pre-Bid Meeting from 20 November 2026 to 28 November 2026 at 11:00 AM.

The Pre-Bid Meeting will provide prospective bidders with an opportunity to seek clarifications regarding the property, eligibility requirements, registration procedures, Earnest Money Deposit (EMD), bidding process and other provisions of the RFP.

NLMC has clarified that all other terms and conditions of the RFP, including the remaining prescribed timelines, shall remain unchanged.

Key Details of the E-Auction

https://eauction.enivida.com

Opportunity for Prospective Homebuyers

Located in Kilpauk, one of Chennai's established residential neighbourhoods, the property offers an opportunity for homebuyers and interested investors seeking residential real estate in a well-connected part of the city.

Prospective bidders are encouraged to review the RFP and relevant property documents carefully. Interested buyers may also visit and inspect the property, subject to the arrangements and conditions prescribed by NLMC, before participating in the e-auction.

NLMC is undertaking publicity and outreach initiatives through newspaper advertisements, radio, digital platforms and other communication channels to ensure wider dissemination of information and encourage participation from prospective buyers.

Advancing Transparent Asset Monetisation

The proposed e-auction forms part of NLMC's continued efforts to facilitate the monetisation of surplus and underutilised public assets through transparent, competitive and technology-enabled processes.

By providing a structured digital auction platform, NLMC aims to enhance market participation, facilitate competitive price discovery and ensure efficient utilisation of public assets.

Interested bidders are advised to refer to the RFP and Corrigendum 1 for complete details regarding the property, participation requirements, applicable terms and conditions and the revised Pre-Bid Meeting schedule.

About NLMC

The National Land Monetization Corporation (NLMC) is a wholly owned Government of India company under the administrative control of the Department of Public Enterprises, Ministry of Finance. NLMC was established to facilitate the monetisation of surplus and underutilised land and building assets of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and other Government entities.

Through structured transaction processes, transparent e-auctions and market-oriented approaches, NLMC seeks to unlock the economic potential of public assets and support their productive utilisation.

2335844.title: Ministry of Railways Observes Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas with Floral Tribute to Bhagwan Birsa Munda
2335844.body_html:
Ministry of Railways
Ministry of Railways Observes Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas with Floral Tribute to Bhagwan Birsa Munda
Posted On: 13 NOV 2026 4:30PM by PIB Delhi

The Ministry of Railways observed Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas today by lighting ceremonial lamps and paying floral tributes to Bhagwan Birsa Munda, the great tribal freedom fighter and revered national hero at Rail Bhawan, New Delhi.

The dignitaries paid their heartfelt tributes to Bhagwan Birsa Munda and recalled his extraordinary contribution to India's freedom struggle and his courageous resistance against British colonial rule. They also remembered his unwavering commitment to safeguarding the rights, dignity and welfare of tribal communities.

The observance of Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas serves as a reminder of the invaluable contributions of tribal freedom fighters and reinforces the spirit of national pride, unity and respect for India's rich tribal heritage.

The programme concluded with a collective tribute to the ideals, courage and enduring legacy of Bhagwan Birsa Munda.

The ceremony was attended by Member (TRS), Member (Finance) and Member (Infra) of the Railway Board. Director Generals (DGs), Secretary, Railway Board, and other senior officers and staff of the Ministry of Railways were also present on the occasion.

2335840.title: Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi  inaugurates, dedicates to the nation, lays the foundation stone and flags off various development projects worth over ₹15,600 crore in Bengaluru, Karnataka
2335840.body_html:
Prime Minister's Office
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi  inaugurates, dedicates to the nation, lays the foundation stone and flags off various development projects worth over ₹15,600 crore in Bengaluru, Karnataka
Infrastructure plays a vital role in the development journey of any nation; Better connectivity creates new avenues for progress, employment, and industry: PM
When developmental opportunities reach every section of society, the fight against poverty is further strengthened; It is a direct result of this that in recent years, nearly 50 crore citizens have emerged from extreme poverty: PM
Following Delhi-NCR and the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, Bengaluru has emerged as the third city in the nation where the metro network has achieved a century: PM
 The success of Namma Metro goes far beyond a single project; it is a powerful reflection of the country's new vision for Ease of Living and Ease of Travel: PM
Just a few days ago, Karnataka received the state's first-ever Vande Bharat Sleeper train; Today, it has been dedicated another Vande Bharat train that connects Karnataka to Goa: PM
Today, India is advancing with the objective of achieving leadership in emerging technologies, from chip to ship, and from AI and data centres to quantum computing: PM
Posted On: 13 NOV 2026 4:17PM by PIB Delhi

Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi today inaugurated, dedicated to the nation, laid the foundation stone, and flagged off various development projects worth over ₹15,600 crore in Bengaluru, Karnataka. Addressing the gathering on the occasion, the Prime Minister extended his greetings in Kannada and bowed in reverence to the city's presiding deity Goddess Annamma Tai and Nadaprabhu Kempegowda, noting that today marks a day to give new momentum to the development journey of Bengaluru and Karnataka through projects spanning connectivity and energy security. “From projects connected with metro and rail to works of energy security, all these projects are going to give new strength to the infrastructure of Karnataka,” asserted Shri Modi.

Emphasizing that infrastructure and improved connectivity generate new avenues for progress, employment, and industry that reach every section of society and strengthen the fight against poverty, as reflected in nearly 50 crore citizens escaping extreme poverty in recent years, the Prime Minister extended his best wishes to the people of Karnataka for the newly launched projects. “They will give new momentum to the building of a Viksit Bharat through a Viksit Karnataka, and at the same time further strengthen the identity of Bengaluru as a Tech City,” affirmed PM Modi.

Highlighting the dedication of the Bengaluru Metro's new Pink Line a short while earlier, the Prime Minister noted that the corridor will significantly improve connectivity to IIM Bengaluru, numerous educational institutions, and major business, technology, and commercial hubs across the city. “Lakhs of people of Bengaluru will not only have convenience in commuting, rather they will also be able to save their money and time,” observed Shri Modi.

Recalling that yesterday marked the Punya Tithi of the late Ananth Kumar, who shared a deep bond with the region, the Prime Minister paid heartfelt tributes to the departed leader. “Seeing this metro line today, his soul too must have been delighted,” remarked PM Modi.

Describing Bengaluru as the Silicon Valley of India that contributes over one-third of the nation's IT exports and serves as a major engine of innovation and economic growth, the Prime Minister stated that the Central Government has prioritized the rapid development of the Bengaluru region and expanded Namma Metro from just 17 kilometers in 2014 to over 100 kilometers today, making Bengaluru the third Indian city after Delhi-NCR and the Mumbai Metropolitan Region to cross the 100-kilometer metro milestone. “This success of Namma Metro is the result of the country's new thinking regarding Ease of Living and Ease of Travel, and the outcome of the country's commitment to make the lives of middle-class families better,” asserted Shri Modi.

Stating that Indian Railways is shedding its colonial-era mindset to build a new legacy where stations, engines, and coaches bear India's distinct identity through Vande Bharat trains and Amrit Bharat stations, including over 60 stations in Karnataka alongside Chamarajanagar, Chikkamagaluru, Sakleshpur, and Subrahmanya Road, the Prime Minister highlighted how these stations blend modernity with sensitivity by offering special amenities for senior citizens and Divyangjans. “The facilities that were earlier found in airports, efforts are now being made to provide those very facilities at railway stations to poor and middle-class families,” noted PM Modi.

Pointing out that India's railway budget has grown manifold over the past 10 to 12 years with a ninefold increase in Karnataka's allocation, the Prime Minister noted that the state received four Amrit stations and two doubling and electrification projects today, alongside a new Vande Bharat train connecting Karnataka with Goa just days after receiving its first Vande Bharat Sleeper train. “Through this train, companions along the entire coastal route of Karnataka, including Mangaluru, will get a new experience of a semi-high-speed train,” observed Shri Modi.

Underscoring that the ongoing war around Iran and the Gulf region has demonstrated the vital importance of energy security, the Prime Minister explained that India weathered this challenging period firmly due to steps taken over the past decade, expanding petrol, diesel, and LPG production, crude oil storage, solar, hydro, and wind energy, near-total rail electrification, and metro networks, and detailed three new Karnataka projects: the Mangaluru LPG Project adding 80,000 metric tonnes of storage capacity, the Devangonthi Marketing Terminal streamlining petrol, diesel, and aviation fuel supply, and the Bengaluru CBG plant producing 13 tonnes of biogas daily. “This will improve waste management and money spent on the import of natural gas will also be saved,” noted PM Modi.

Highlighting that reliable electricity generation is essential as India strives for global leadership across new technologies from chips to ships and from AI and data centers to quantum computing, the Prime Minister noted that the nation is expanding its nuclear power plants to achieve clean energy goals. “Today India's renewable energy capacity has exceeded 300 gigawatts,” observed Shri Modi.

Pointing out that Central schemes are transforming Indian citizens from electricity consumers into electricity producers, the Prime Minister noted that over 60 lakh households nationwide, including more than 40,000 families in Karnataka, have installed rooftop solar plants with Central assistance of around 80,000 rupees per family under the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, while irrigation through over 8 lakh solar pumps is being arranged for Karnataka's farmers under the PM KUSUM Yojana to cut power costs and generate new income and jobs. “Meaning, the Annadatas of Karnataka are now also becoming Urjadatas,” remarked PM Modi.

Observing that purposeful national execution, public participation, and proper utilization of taxpayer money under the post-2014 resolve of Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas have expanded the middle class and created a new Aspirational Class seeking home appliances, two-wheelers, quality education, nutrition, healthcare, and tourism experiences, the Prime Minister pointed out that these rising aspirations are driving new industrial and job growth across automobiles, electronics, tourism, and services, making the Neo Middle Class a major engine of India's economic growth. “The interest of this Neo Middle Class, which is present in large numbers in Karnataka and in Bengaluru as well, is among the priorities of the Central Government,” affirmed Shri Modi.

Stating that the Central Government is working continuously to boost middle-class savings and put more disposable income in their hands, the Prime Minister highlighted measures such as exempting annual income up to 12 lakh rupees from income tax, revising TDS rules to benefit senior citizens and rental earners, and lowering the cost of everyday goods through next-generation GST reforms. “By abolishing GST on personal health and life insurance, we made insurance more affordable,” noted PM Modi.

Concluding his address by stating that today's projects in Karnataka will further accelerate the nation's developmental trajectory and extending his best wishes to the people, the Prime Minister emphasized the government's commitment to empowering middle-class families. “Our effort is that the savings of the middle class increase, their purchasing power becomes strong, and along with fulfilling the dreams of their family, they also become partners in the economic progress of the country,” affirmed Shri Modi.

A major boost to Karnataka's growth! Projects worth over ₹15,000 crore are being launched today to strengthen connectivity and energy security. https://t.co/jfMwD06wCK

2335657.title: English rendering of PM's address at the Kisan Tak Bharat Agriculture Conference
2335657.body_html:
Prime Minister's Office
English rendering of PM's address at the Kisan Tak Bharat Agriculture Conference
Posted On: 12 NOV 2026 10:09PM by PIB Delhi

You also have my heartfelt greetings on this sacred festival of Diwali, and with the programme of Chhathi Maiya also approaching, I extend my very best wishes for that as well. My greetings to all of you.

Chairman and Editor-in-Chief of the India Today Group, Shri Arun Puri ji, the agricultural scientists, agri-entrepreneurs, farmer friends, and all distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen who have come from across the country for this programme.

First of all, I wholeheartedly congratulate the India Today Group for this innovative initiative. When the country launched the cleanliness campaign, the India Today Group participated in it very enthusiastically. Now you have organised this Kisan Mela, and dedicated two full days to it. This is a very positive beginning. I congratulate all of you. And Arun ji speaks such excellent Hindi, so double congratulations for that.

Friends,

This event is taking place at a time when the country is in a festive mood. Two or three days ago, we celebrated the festival of Diwali, and now the spirit of the Chhath Mahaparva is all around us. The festival of Chhath is deeply connected with agricultural life, and in our country, most festivals are linked with farming and agriculture. Bihu, Pongal, Onam, Baisakhi, Sarhul, Pola, many such festivals are connected with agriculture. In other words, farming is our culture, our tradition, and the foundation of our social life.

Friends,

From the Red Fort, I had spoken about the seven streams of strength for a Viksit India, and among these, agriculture is a principal stream. Building a Viksit India is simply not possible without developing agriculture, without making farming smarter, and without empowering farmers. That is why the importance of such farmer conferences becomes even greater.

Friends,

You can understand the relationship between farming and the country's progress through two important facts. Recently, a World Bank study on poverty was released, and it is being discussed across the world. It states that within just 12–13 years, 50 crore poor people in India have defeated poverty. It also states that poverty has declined very rapidly in villages. This means that a large number of small farmers and agricultural labourers have overcome poverty. Now look at the coincidence. During the past decade, India's agricultural growth rate has remained above 4 percent. This is the first decade after Independence in which the country's agriculture sector has achieved an average growth rate of more than 4 percent, for the first time since Independence. And during this same period, a large number of poor people in villages have defeated poverty. But unfortunately, people trapped in angles and agendas of news coverage fail to notice this achievement of the country.

Friends,

Those engaged in farming and experts connected with agriculture know how necessary continuous change in agricultural policies and methods is. Those who governed for decades became satisfied merely because the country's farmers had filled the grain warehouses of the nation. But what did farmers receive after that? Merely filling grain warehouses is not enough. Over time, the world changed, markets changed, people's needs changed, eating habits changed, the weather changed, and technology changed. Along with these changes, we needed to empower our farmers in a new way. But earlier, even this was not given attention.

Friends,

Over the past decade, the country took steps to match this pace, and the results are before all of us. Today, India exports agricultural products worth more than four lakh crore rupees every year, and this money is increasing the income of our farmers. Today, India is number one in the world in milk production. Today, India is number one in pulse production. India is number one in jute production. India has also become number one in rice production. It is number two in the world in wheat production. It is number two in the production of cotton, fruits, and vegetables. It is number two in fish production, and India is also the world's largest producer of millets. These are not just statistics. They show how much the capability of India's farmers has grown.

Friends,

One more thing is necessary for the prosperity of India's farmers. It is necessary that they do not remain dependent only on traditional crops such as wheat, rice, and sugarcane. I repeat, farmer brothers should not remain dependent only on wheat, rice, and sugarcane. Therefore, the government is also placing emphasis on other crops and other activities related to agriculture. Let me remind the India Today Group of something. The word “revolution”, kranti, is something the India Today Group is particularly fond of. Therefore, I am now going to talk about a few revolutions.

Friends,

There was a time when the country took a historic step towards self-reliance in food grain production through the Green Revolution. After that, the White Revolution made India the world's largest milk producer. Today, I will give you some more figures that show how this journey is now moving forward with remarkable momentum. Over the past decade, India's milk production has increased by nearly 70 percent, 70 percent. Egg production has also increased by nearly 90 percent, 90 percent. And if we talk about the Blue Revolution, India's fish production has more than doubled in a decade. New opportunities have emerged in the field of beekeeping through the Sweet Revolution. Honey production has increased from around 80 thousand tonnes to 150 thousand tonnes. In horticulture as well, India's production has increased from 280 million tonnes to more than 350 million tonnes.

Friends,

When we connect all these revolutions with a broader vision, multiple sources of income are created for the country's farmers, and this is very essential for the future of agriculture. Let me give you another example. Another revolution, the solar power revolution. This revolution has transformed the food provider into an energy provider. Under the PM-KUSUM Scheme, nearly 12 lakh solar pumps have already been distributed. This is reducing farmers' electricity bills, and farmers have also begun earning income by installing solar plants on their fields. Along with production, we have also focused on productivity and on farmers' profits.

Friends,

Recently, I completed 25 years as the head of government. When I was the Chief Minister of Gujarat, I was continuously working to modernise agriculture even then. At that time, I started large agricultural festivals. I remember that in May and June, in temperatures of 40–45 degrees Celsius, hundreds of agricultural scientists, agricultural experts, and progressive farmers would come together. We would prepare Kisan Raths and travel in them. We would go to villages and to fields. We would visit farmers' fields and interact directly with them. What type of soil the area had, what the availability of water was, which crops could perform well there, what kind of farming was required, every such issue would be discussed directly with farmers. Our effort was that the knowledge present in scientists' laboratories should directly reach farmers' fields. In other words, we moved forward with the concept of Lab to Land, and Gujarat's farmers benefited greatly from it.

Friends,

The experience from my Gujarat days has been extremely useful after coming to the central government. In 2014, there were only a few hundred soil-testing laboratories in the country. Today, their number has increased to more than 8,400. Just as pathology laboratories are expanding in medical science, today soil-testing laboratories are expanding. Today, there are more than 750 Krishi Vigyan Kendras across the country. We are also prioritising the protection of animals from diseases. To protect livestock from Foot and Mouth Disease, more than eight crore farmers' animals have received free vaccinations. During COVID, we provided free vaccines, and everyone remembers that. But this is Modi; he provides free vaccines even to animals.

Friends,

Often, some people with old ways of thinking believe that the use of large-scale technology will not be possible in our villages. The Namo Drone Didis have proved such people wrong. Once, while speaking with all the Drone Didis through video conferencing, I was talking to a daughter from a village, perhaps in Jharkhand. She told me, “Now my status has changed.” I asked, “Why?” She said, “The entire village calls me a pilot, and even my younger brothers-in-law call me ‘Pilot Bhabhi’.” Just imagine how much self-respect increases. At present, the Namo Drone Didis are using drones for spraying fertilisers and pesticides. Now the scope of their use is also being expanded.

Friends,

Today’s India is also expanding the role of engineering in agriculture. Our agricultural scientists, engineers, and youth are together developing such tools and machines that are reducing the cost of farming. In some places, machines are being developed that are making sowing and harvesting easier. And I would especially like to urge the people from industry present here, those engaged in manufacturing equipment for farmers, as well as our startup founders, that whatever equipment you build from now on should be powered by solar energy, because we are taking solar power to every farm. Just as the whole world has now rushed towards electric vehicles, I am in favour of making every type of agricultural tool solar-powered. And I am also making considerable efforts in that direction. But I would urge all MSMEs and small-scale industries to focus on this. This is going to become a very large area of revolution. Not only that, sensor-based equipment equipped with AI technology is now being developed that can provide precise information to farmers and can be affordable even for the smallest farmers. Arrangements are now being developed for soil testing through mobile phones. You simply place a little soil on the mobile-based device, and your phone immediately provides a report identifying which crop your soil is suitable for, how much fertilizer is required, and what type of fertilizer is needed. In other words, just see how rapidly change is taking place. Today, from agricultural engineering to agri-startups, India is full of opportunities. We must transform our food providers into agri-preneurs, that is, agricultural entrepreneurs. Work is now progressing rapidly across the country on how value addition can take place right where production happens.

Friends,

In the past few years, small farmers, working together with the government, have built a large network of 10,000 FPOs, that is, Farmer Producer Organizations. These are turning groups of small farmers into value creators and connecting them with the food-processing business. I clearly remember one incident from my days in Gujarat. In Gujarat, we introduced the Jyotigram Yojana. We separated agricultural feeders from domestic feeders and began supplying as much electricity to farmers as possible. This greatly benefited farmers. There are some villages near Gandhinagar where most people cultivate chillies. But farmers there faced a problem. If production increased, prices would fall, and if production declined, earnings would decline. They suffered in both situations. If too many chillies were produced, they could not sell them. But after the arrival of electricity through the Jyotigram Yojana, they started converting chillies into red chilli powder. They packaged that powder, got advertisements made, printed photographs of personalities on the packaging, and began selling chilli powder on a large scale. Through this value addition, they became highly successful earners. Earlier, they could not even obtain a proper price for their chillies, but now their products became brands. This shows what becomes possible when attention is given to every small aspect. Efforts to connect small farmers with export markets are also progressing rapidly.

Friends,

Our policy and our intent are absolutely clear. It is our priority that farming should not become a burden on farmers. To ensure affordable fertilizers for farmers, the country has spent ₹16 lakh crore over the last 12 years. Friends, this is an enormous figure. Sixteen lakh crore rupees is more than the annual budget of many countries. Amid the war currently taking place around Iran and the Gulf countries, a bag of DAP fertilizer that costs ₹5,000 is being made available to Indian farmers for only ₹1,300. A bag of urea that costs ₹3,000 in the international market is being provided to Indian farmers for less than ₹300.

Friends,

I would like to mention one more subject, and I have spoken about this before as well. For your network, what I am about to say today is exclusive.

Friends,

When the war situation in West Asia was escalating, the price of crude oil rose from 70 dollars to 122 dollars per barrel within just a few weeks. At that time, India also faced a major challenge. India was in a situation where diesel prices should have been increased by at least ₹50 per litre. An increase of ₹50 per litre had become necessary. At that time, the government took a decision in the interest of farmers. We decided that the full burden of the shock in international markets would not be passed on to citizens and farmers. The government increased diesel prices by only ₹7 per litre, whereas the required increase was ₹50. The government itself absorbed a burden of ₹43 per litre. In neighbouring countries as well, diesel prices had increased by 40 to 50 percent. But that did not happen in India. Since then and up to today, the government has been bearing a loss of ₹14,000 crore every month. Every month. Yet we did not allow harm to come to the country's farmers. When the welfare of farmers is the highest priority, when there is a spirit of Citizen Devo Bhava, such sensitive decisions are taken.

Friends,

Amid so many discussions about the national interest, I am sure the people of Aaj Tak must be wondering that no negative headline has emerged so far. So perhaps now we should discuss something that can become a headline. Until now, I have been talking about the country, and perhaps that has not attracted as much media attention. So now let me talk about controversy.

Friends,

Nowadays, some people pull the Constitution out of their pockets. The country understands very well what they are doing. They seem to think that the nation's Constitution and democracy are sitting in their pocket. Even while not being in power, they remain intoxicated with the mindset of power. But when these very people were in power, what were their actions like? Let me narrate a small incident.

Friends,

You may remember that there was a time when people in the media used to rank the best-performing states. In one such ranking related to the economy, Gujarat was ranked number one, and at that time I was the Chief Minister of Gujarat. The institution that gave Gujarat the number one ranking was named after a former Prime Minister of India. That hint is enough; you can find the name yourselves. This ranking was based on research conducted by some of the country's most respected economists. But the people sitting in power in Delhi did not like Gujarat receiving that recognition. They formally instructed those conducting the research that things could not continue this way. They said that from then onward, no report could be published without their approval first.

Friends,

That was the situation then, and today those very people go around delivering lectures on tolerance and democracy. And when exactly did this happen? What happened after that? You can research and find those details yourselves. Let me now move towards concluding my remarks.

Friends,

Without doubt, the achievements of the country’s farmers over the past years have been remarkable. To build a Viksit India, we now have to expand our efforts even further. We must create a future where farmers are prosperous, villages are prosperous, and agriculture is modern and profitable. I am confident that the deliberations taking place here will benefit the country. The government will also work upon the best suggestions and solutions that emerge from here. And since I have come among you today, I would certainly like to make one appeal. At the beginning, Anjana ji said in her introductory remarks that farmers are connected to two things: the food provider and Mother Earth. I want to ask my farmer brothers and sisters: are we really protecting this Mother Earth of ours? Ask yourselves honestly. The way we are destroying Mother Earth through excessive use of chemicals, and we are her children. We are killing this mother before our own eyes. If we do not wake up in time, if we do not make efforts to save Mother Earth, then the mother who nourishes us today may one day leave our hands. Such a situation could arise. That is why the government has emphasized natural farming. Those who have experimented with natural farming have achieved great success. A single cow can provide sufficient manure for natural farming on 30 acres of land. No chemical inputs are required. Many such subjects must have emerged during your discussions today. Therefore, I appeal to all farmers that we should move towards chemical-free farming. I am not talking about organic farming; I am talking about natural farming, and every farmer can adopt it easily. We can take steps to save our soil by becoming free from chemicals. One challenge with our farmer brothers and sisters is that until they see something with their own eyes, they do not accept it. No matter how many long speeches are delivered, farmers do not simply accept something. They believe only after seeing it. Otherwise, all that stays in their minds is that they must apply the yellow powder, use the green bottle, use the green container, bring the red container, and if the neighbour uses two bags, they will use two bags too; if the neighbour uses four sacks, they will use four sacks too. This is the responsibility of all of us, and especially of progressive farmers, to free them from this mindset. We must help them move towards chemical-free natural farming. The first task is to save our Mother Earth. This mother is capable of providing everything we need. She will never let us feel any shortage, provided we protect her. We are the children of Mother Earth. It is our duty to fulfil this responsibility as her sons and daughters, as the children of Mother Earth. With this confidence, I extend my best wishes to all of you. I also congratulate the India Today Group. You have undertaken a task that will greatly help the nation in the years ahead.

Thank you very much.

DISCLAIMER: This is the approximate translation of the Prime Minister’s address. Original address was delivered in Hindi.

************

MJPS/SS/VJ/ST

2335622.title: 57th IFFI to Bring Together Global Cinema and Creative Voices in Goa from 20 to 28 November 2026
2335622.body_html:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
57th IFFI to Bring Together Global Cinema and Creative Voices in Goa from 20 to 28 November 2026
Goa Chief Minister Dr. Pramod Sawant to Grace Curtain Raiser Press Conference; Festival to Unveil Highlights of ‘Stories Without Borders’
Posted On: 12 NOV 2026 9:14PM by PIB Mumbai

Goa, 12 November 2026

 

The 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) will bring together filmmakers, cinema enthusiasts and creative voices from across the world in Goa from 20 to 28 November 2026, under the theme ‘Stories Without Borders’.

The Curtain Raiser Press Conference of the festival will be held tomorrow, 13 November 2026, at Taj Cidade de Goa Horizon, Goa, to unveil the highlights, major attractions and key programmes of the forthcoming edition.

Hon’ble Chief Minister of Goa, Dr. Pramod Sawant, will grace the occasion. Smt. Delilah Lobo, Vice Chairperson, Entertainment Society of Goa (ESG), will also be present, along with Shri Chanchal Kumar, Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting; Chairperson, National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) Sh G Krishnakumar; Managing Director, NFDC Sh Dhiraj Singh; Shri Ashutosh Gowariker, Festival Director, IFFI 2026; and the Chairpersons of the Festival Jury.

Reflecting IFFI’s growing global reach, the 57th edition will present an expansive and diverse programme celebrating the richness of Indian and international cinema. The press conference will share details of the festival's offerings and provide a glimpse into the cinematic experiences and creative exchanges planned for audiences and participants from across the world.

With its theme ‘Stories Without Borders’, IFFI 2026 seeks to celebrate cinema as a medium that transcends geographical and cultural boundaries, connecting audiences through diverse stories and shared human experiences.

 

* * *

PIB Panaji | Nana Meshram/Riyas Babu/Darshana Rane

2335599.title: 2nd Edition of the National Tribal Literary Festival 2026 begins in New Delhi: “From Oral Tradition to Contemporary Tribal Literature
2335599.body_html:
Ministry of Tribal Affairs
2nd Edition of the National Tribal Literary Festival 2026 begins in New Delhi: “From Oral Tradition to Contemporary Tribal Literature
“Preserving tribal languages and oral traditions is central to building Viksit Bharat 2047.” – Union Minister of Tribal Affairs
Two-day festival organised by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to celebrate Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas Pakhwada
Tribal writers, poets, researchers and language experts from across the country to share their works and ideas
Day 1 sessions on tribal literature, a poets’ meet and tribal folklore focused on living tribal values, community consent in documenting cultural heritage, linking state tribal portals and digitising archival holdings
Posted On: 12 NOV 2026 7:57PM by PIB Delhi

Under the leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister, the Union Cabinet declared 15th November, the birth anniversary of Bhagwan Birsa Munda, as Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas, to celebrate the rich tribal heritage and bring the contributions of tribal heroes into the national consciousness. Carrying forward this vision, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Government of India, inaugurated the second edition of the two-day National Tribal Literary Festival today at the India Habitat Centre, New Delhi. Held on the occasion of Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas Pakhwada, the festival celebrates tribal literature, languages, and oral traditions under the inspiring guidance of the Hon’ble Prime Minister. Bringing together tribal writers, poets, researchers and language experts, the festival celebrates the evolution of tribal expression from oral tradition to contemporary literature. In line with the Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s mantra of “Virasat bhi, Vikas bhi,” it reaffirms the vision of a Viksit Bharat 2047 that draws strength from its heritage and ensures that tribal languages and knowledge systems are preserved, promoted and woven into the national mainstream.

The festival was inaugurated by the Hon’ble Union Minister of Tribal Affairs, Shri Jual Oram, along with the Hon’ble Minister of State for Tribal Affairs, Shri Durgadas Uikey, the Hon’ble Member of NITI Aayog, Dr. Joram Aniya, Padma Shri Shri Chamu Krishna Shastry, Chairman, Bharatiya Bhasha Samiti, Smt. Ranjana Chopra, Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, and Shri Anant Prakash Pandey, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, by lighting the ceremonial lamp. Tribal writers, researchers and language experts from across the country were present.

Welcoming the dignitaries, tribal writers and experts, the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Shri Anant Prakash Pandey, said that the knowledge and traditions of tribal communities must be given national recognition, and that new and young tribal writers have to act as a bridge in translating the rich oral traditions of their communities into written literature, carrying the wisdom of their ancestors to future generations and to the wider nation.

In her opening remarks, the Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Smt. Ranjana Chopra, said that the festival gives tribal writers and publishers a platform and creates an opportunity for dialogue between senior and young writers. She stressed the importance of preserving the languages and cultural traditions of tribal communities in the country and said that oral traditions must be documented before they disappear. She said the festival aims to give tribal heritage national recognition and secure it for future generations. Noting that this is the second edition of the National Tribal Literary Festival, she said that this will continue as an annual feature in all the Pakhwada periods to come.

Padma Shri Shri Chamu Krishna Shastry, Chairman, Bharatiya Bhasha Samiti, said that a nation’s awakening rests on knowledge (Gyana Shakti), action (Kriya Shakti) and willpower (Iccha Shakti). He said that with willpower, the nation can be awakened to build a grand, prosperous and united India. He stressed on unity in diversity and how language can strengthen national integrity.

Dr. Joram Aniya, Hon’ble Member, NITI Aayog, describing the festival as a historic gathering celebrating India’s self-respect, ancient traditions and tribal pride, paid homage to Bhagwan Birsa Munda and said his Ulgulan was a struggle to protect tribal culture, language, traditions and identity. She said, “The real and living literature of India is not found only in books, but resides in the hearts of the people in the form of folk songs, lullabies and stories of our tribal societies.” She complimented the Ministry of Tribal Affairs for curating such a platform for the documentation of tribal literature.

Shri Durgadas Uikey, Hon’ble Minister of State for Tribal Affairs, expressed gratitude for the Hon’ble Prime Minister’s visionary leadership in honouring tribal heritage, saying, “The Hon’ble Prime Minister has taken the historic initiative of celebrating the birth anniversary of Bhagwan Birsa Munda as Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas. It is a resolve to connect the country’s tribal heroes, freedom fighters, social reformers and their glorious heritage with the national consciousness.” He presented a ten-point (Das Bindu) framework on the essence of tribal oral traditions, covering folktales, folk songs, heroic sagas, myths, proverbs, riddles, rituals and prayers.

Shri Jual Oram, Hon’ble Union Minister of Tribal Affairs, said that systematic documentation of the literature, folk songs, folktales and oral traditions of tribal languages is essential for their preservation, and that this effort must include not only writers but also lyricists, musicians, folk artists and digital content creators. Noting that many tribal languages have no script and some dialects are on the verge of extinction, he said the absence of a script must not become a barrier, and that oral traditions can be preserved through available Indian languages. He informed that the Ministry will collaborate with the Sahitya Akademi and other organisations working in this field to promote and preserve tribal literature

The first session, “Tribal Literature: From Community Memory to Contemporary Expression”, explored tribal literature as a continuum encompassing oral traditions, cultural memory and contemporary literary creativity. The session was moderated by Prof. Anil Kumar Boro, with Ms. K. Vasamalli, Dr. Damayanti Beshra and Dr. Dharmendra Pare as discussants.

Ms. K. Vasamalli, representing the Toda community of the Nilgiris, said that without language, a community’s traditions and culture cannot develop. She spoke of her efforts to document the endangered Toda language, which has only about 2,000 speakers, through radio recordings, her published work and a 5,700-word dictionary created using the International Phonetic Alphabet and modified Tamil script. Highlighting the close bond between the Toda people and nature, she said the community does not practise idol worship, and that for them “the mountains are the temple of the gods.” She also shared ecological markers embedded in Toda culture, including sacred mountains and rivers and the reverence for native flora used by priests and in clan naming.

Prof. Anil Kumar Boro, reflecting on concerns about the erosion of traditional values due to modernisation and growing individualism, cited the example of the Mizo people in Aizawl, who maintain strict self-discipline even in city traffic. He said, “We may be following a modern urbanised way of life, but still we can follow the values that our tribal forefathers had been following and preserving.”

Dr. Dharmendra Pare said that while memories may fade, knowledge, awareness, conduct and traditions are never destroyed. He noted that the unlettered wisdom once shared in fields and homes is being replaced by screens, and illustrated the essence of tribal consciousness through a festival in which honey is shared by the entire community rather than consumed individually, a Gond story of siblings who turned away from a city market because there was no place for their gods, and the ethical hunting practices of the Baiga and Pardhi communities, who do not hunt pregnant birds. He said true preservation lies in understanding and living these values, and not merely in compiling dictionaries.

The second session, “The Joy of Life: Tribal Poets’ Meet”, was held in two parts, with poetry readings by poets from different tribal languages. The session was moderated by Prof. Kanji Patel. Dr. Rekha Kharadi, Dr. Jitendrabhai Vajirsing Vasava, Ms. Yashoda Murmu, Dr. Jomyir Jini, Prof. Snehlata Negi and Ms. Parwati Tirkey presented their poems.

The third session, “Tribal Folklore: Songs, Myths, Tales, Proverbs, Sayings and Oral Narratives”, explored the diversity of tribal oral traditions, including songs, myths, riddles and tales. The session was moderated by Prof. Sylvanus Lamare, with Dr. Lisa Lomdak, Mr. Anuja Mohan Pradhan and Ms. Swati Anand as discussants.

Drawing on her research in Arunachal Pradesh, Dr. Lisa Lomdak spoke of the custodians of oral traditions, such as the Nyibu, Midi and Abatani, and Njik-Njegam, who preserve knowledge through memory rather than writing. She highlighted the role of women as repositories of oral tradition, preserving narratives through songs during daily chores, marriages and funerals. She underlined that researchers must publish sacred traditions and knowledge only with explicit community permission.

Mr. Anuja Mohan Pradhan, representing the Kui-speaking community of Odisha, said that the Kui language has a rich oral heritage of creation myths, riddles and songs, but is gradually disappearing due to the lack of a formal script and the pressures of modern multilingualism. He shared a traditional Kui riddle and folk tales, including one that symbolises how tribal communities risk losing their roots and culture to outside influences.

Ms. Swati Anand shared the cultural heritage of Bastar, Chhattisgarh, including the Bastar Madai festival and local legends of protective deities, which continue to live in community memory and practice.

In his concluding remarks, the moderator made three suggestions: linking all state tribal affairs websites to the Ministry’s main portal; digitising and making accessible information on tribal communities available with the international institutions and libraries; and scientifically studying and documenting tribal scientific and engineering knowledge, such as the living root bridges of Meghalaya.

On Day 2, the festival will hold sessions on oral epics and heroic traditions and on oral tradition in multilingual education, along with story and poetry readings in various tribal languages, followed by the valedictory session.

*****
